walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 1: Guided Literary Analysis — a core area of English Literature.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 1: Guided Literary Analysis brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 1: Guided Literary Analysis.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Who coined the term ostranenie (defamiliarisation) in 1917?
options: Viktor Shklovsky
Roman Jakobson
Boris Eikhenbaum
Yuri Tynyanov

mcqs.q: Whose 1946 essay attacked the intentional fallacy?
options: Wimsatt and Beardsley
Brooks and Warren
Frye and Bloom
Empson and Richards

mcqs.q: What defines epic poetry as a genre?
options: Long narrative poems on heroic subjects, in elevated style, often invoking a muse, in medias res openings, and treating events of national or cosmic significance.
Epic means any story with a battle in it.
Epic means any poem that is very long.
Enjambment is when a poem uses no punctuation at all.
Enjambment is when a poem has very long lines.
When a sentence or phrase runs over from one line of poetry to the next without a punctuated pause, creating flow or surprise across the line break.
Enjambment is when a poem uses no punctuation at all.
Epic means any story with a battle in it.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
Epic means any story with a battle in it.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
